items.title: AI, Specialization, and the Organization of Knowledge Work: Evidence from Legal Services
items.desc: Develops a framework for how AI-cheapened expertise reallocates work across providers and finds, in U.S. legal services, a 6.6-point rise in non-prisoner self-representation across 89 federal districts, while the largest law firms grew revenue 13% on flat billable hours. [arXiv econ.GN, submitted 2026-11-17]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Today's paper is based on the abstract only, so we'll keep it short. It asks what happens to professional-service firms when AI makes specialized knowledge cheaper.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: And the setting is U.S. legal services. Why law?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Because clients can substitute in several ways: do the work themselves, bring it in-house, or move to cheaper outside providers. The authors build a framework linking those choices to how specialist firms price.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: What's the surprising prediction?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: If the work leaving premium firms is the more price-sensitive work, the work that remains is less price-sensitive, so premium firms can actually raise their markups even as their share of work declines.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: So what do the data show?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Across eighty-nine federal districts, a difference-in-differences analysis finds a 6.6 percentage point increase in self-representation by non-prisoners, relative to prisoner petitions, by fiscal 2025. Lawyer employment shows no clear shift toward client firms, and the largest law firms reported thirteen percent revenue growth in 2025 with nearly flat billable hours.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Any caveats?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The authors note much of the reallocation predates generative AI, and legal AI benchmarks still show trouble with complex multi-step work.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: So the takeaway: cheaper expertise doesn't automatically mean in-house work or falling prices for premium services.

items.title: Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading
items.desc: Presents an agent-native trading framework unifying research, backtesting, paper trading and optional broker execution, with traceable results and an explicit authority gate between research and live trading. [arXiv cs.AI, submitted 2026-11-18]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: This one is based on the abstract only. Vibe-Trading is a framework for building and evaluating AI trading agents.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: What problem does it tackle?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Most AI agents use fairly static workflows and struggle to keep reliable state as the world changes. In trading, prices, news, positions and capital all move, so a result is only useful if it's tied to the right time, data snapshot and execution context.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: So what do they build?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: An all-in-one workspace that unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration and optional broker execution.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: And the central idea?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: An architecture where every result keeps its source, time scope, configuration and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records allow reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: In short: traceable, reproducible agent results that only act on real money under explicit authority.

items.title: When Price Charts Rhyme: Historical Visual Retrieval for Stock Return Prediction
items.desc: Uses a vision model to retrieve historically similar stock price charts; the retrieved neighbors' returns predict the cross-section, and return-aligned training more than doubles the strategy's Sharpe ratio. [arXiv q-fin.ST, submitted 2026-11-18]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: This summary is based on the abstract only. The paper asks whether stocks with visually similar price charts go on to have similar returns.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: How do they test that?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: They use a vision model to retrieve each stock's most similar historical charts from three decades of U.S. price histories, then look at what those neighbors earned afterward.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: And does it work?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Even a model pretrained only on natural images retrieves neighbors whose returns predict the cross-section of stock returns. Aligning the representation with subsequent returns more than doubles the strategy's Sharpe ratio, and beats a convolutional network trained directly on chart images.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Where does the signal come from?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: It's concentrated among stocks with greater limits to arbitrage, and it seems to identify temporary selling pressure that partially reverts. A sparse autoencoder traces the signal to recurring visual states.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: And it's transparent, since each forecast links back to dated historical charts.

items.title: PIRanNN: Random-Feature Pricing and Calibration under Jump-Diffusion and Stochastic-Volatility Models
items.desc: Prices and calibrates options with a one-hidden-layer random-feature network fit by least squares, matching a physics-informed network's accuracy in seconds rather than about half an hour on its test problems. [arXiv q-fin.CP, submitted 2026-11-15]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Abstract-only again. This paper uses a one-hidden-layer random-feature network to price and calibrate options.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: What makes it different from a typical neural network?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The inner weights are fixed and random, so fitting is a single regularized least-squares problem, with no iterative training.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: How accurate is it?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Subtracting the Black-Scholes price cuts error for jump models by about two orders of magnitude. It's about as accurate as a standard finite-difference scheme at the same run time, and matches a recent physics-informed network's accuracy in seconds instead of about half an hour.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: What about calibration?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Without the subtraction, jump parameters can be off by up to fifty percent; with it, within three percent. For Heston and SABR, pricing errors are about one percent and parameters within about fifteen percent.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: So a solver can fit quotes and still return wrong parameters if pricing error isn't small enough.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Right. The paper covers Merton and Kou jump models, where the jump integral of each feature is explicit so no numerical quadrature is needed, and Heston and SABR stochastic volatility models as an applicability study.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: And one factorization of the least-squares matrix gives the price at every state and time, its Greeks, and exact derivatives with respect to the model parameters for gradient-based calibration.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: That's the practical appeal: fast, simple, and with a clear lesson that pricing accuracy matters for calibration, not just for fitting prices. Again, this is from the abstract only.
